# Profilers (nsys, ncu)

The `autocuda:discover` skill recorded the exact invocations that work
in this environment in the **Profiling** section of `<data-dir>/environment.md`.
Use those verbatim — substitute the benchmark command into the `<cmd>`
placeholder. The defaults below are a fallback only; the environment file
takes precedence.

Every profiler invocation must be wrapped in `autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <cmd>` so
it takes the shared GPU lock exclusively (blocking every other slice or
exclusive caller on that lock until done). See the SKILL.md *Concurrency*
section.

## Nsight Systems (nsys)

Use for system-level analysis: kernel launch overhead, host-device
synchronization, memory transfers, API call timing, multi-stream
concurrency, and overall timeline. Start here to understand where time
is spent at a high level.

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- nsys profile --stats=true <benchmark_command>
```

The `--stats=true` flag prints a summary of GPU kernels, CUDA API calls,
and memory operations sorted by time. Look for unexpected gaps,
serialization points, or dominant API calls.

A capture with no kernel data is a failed profile, not a finding.

## Nsight Compute (ncu)

Use for kernel-level analysis: memory throughput, compute throughput,
occupancy, warp stalls, instruction mix, and cache behavior. Use this
when you know which kernel to optimize and need to understand its
internal bottlenecks.

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- ncu --set full <benchmark_command>
```

NCU adds massive overhead per kernel launch. If the benchmark launches
many kernels, filter to the one you care about:

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- ncu --set full --kernel-name <regex> --launch-skip <N> --launch-count 1 <benchmark_command>
```

The default output prints each section's metrics followed by **rule
results** — actionable suggestions and bottleneck diagnoses generated by
NCU's built-in rules engine. Focus on these rule results to guide your
next optimization hypothesis.

## Sudo failover

**If `nsys` or `ncu` fails, re-run it with `sudo`.** The most common
failure modes — `ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM`, "the user does not have permission
to profile on the target device", "access to performance counters is
disabled", and generic permission errors reading performance counters —
are all fixed by running the profiler as root. Prefix the invocation
with `sudo -E` so env vars (`PATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`,
`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, etc.) are preserved:

```bash
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- sudo -E ncu --set full <benchmark_command>
autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- sudo -E nsys profile --stats=true <benchmark_command>
```

See [NVIDIA's ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM guide](https://developer.nvidia.com/ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM)
for background. Never abandon profiling just because the tool reported
an error on the first try — `sudo` almost always resolves it. If sudo
also fails, try the remediations in the `autocuda:discover` skill
(adjusting `PATH`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `kernel.perf_event_paranoid`,
etc.) before giving up, and update `<data-dir>/environment.md`'s Profiling
section with whatever finally worked so subsequent trials don't repeat
the troubleshooting.

## Output naming

Profiles land under `<data-dir>/profiles/<tag>/`. The filename always
ends in the producing commit's full SHA so `autocuda init brief` can
glob the directory for a parent commit's profile and hand it to the
next worker:

- `baseline-<sha>.nsys-rep`, `baseline-<sha>.ncu-rep` — the manager's
  baseline profile. `<sha>` is the baseline commit (`$BASELINE`).
- `brief-<K>-trial-<#>-<sha>.nsys-rep` and
  `brief-<K>-trial-<#>-<sha>.ncu-rep` — a brief's
  per-trial profile, where `<K>` is the brief id. `<sha>` is the
  trial's commit SHA (captured after `git commit`, before the
  profile is written).

The `<sha>` token is what `autocuda init brief` matches
against; the brief / trial tokens are for human readability.

===== libraries =====
# Libraries over hand-written kernels

**Strongly prefer optimized libraries over hand-written CUDA kernels.** NVIDIA's libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN, cuFFT, etc.) are tuned by domain experts across generations of hardware. A hand-written kernel that beats a library call is rare and fragile — it may win on one GPU and lose on the next. Your first instinct when optimizing a hand-written kernel should be: can I replace this with a library call?

Only write custom kernels when:

- No library covers the operation.
- **Fusion**: multiple library calls can be fused into a single kernel to eliminate intermediate memory traffic, reducing launch overhead and memory round-trips.
- Profiling proves the library version is the bottleneck *and* you have a concrete hypothesis for why a custom kernel would be faster.

## Which library?

The CUDA ecosystem offers libraries at many levels. Prefer the highest level that meets your performance needs:

- **CCCL (Thrust / CUB / libcudacxx)** — parallel algorithms, block/warp-level primitives, C++ standard library facilities for device code.
- **CUTLASS** — templated GEMM and convolution building blocks; prefer over hand-rolled matrix math.
- **cuBLAS / cuBLASLt** — dense linear algebra; hard to beat for standard BLAS operations.
- **cuDNN** — deep learning primitives (convolutions, normalization, attention); use when the workload fits.
- **cuFFT / cuSPARSE / cuRAND / cuSOLVER** — domain-specific libraries for FFTs, sparse linear algebra, random number generation, and dense solvers.
- **Cooperative groups** — flexible thread grouping beyond the traditional block/warp model.
- **PTX intrinsics / inline assembly** — last resort for squeezing out final percentage points when profiling proves it necessary.
